query: For transition-metal catalysts, formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis explaining what governs catalytic activity, selectivity, or durability and why. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In dilute alloy catalysts, when a small amount of a reactive dopant (e.g. Pt) is preferentially embedded at the metal–support interface (i.e. in the subsurface), it remotely modulates the electronic structure of the host metal (e.g. Cu) by downshifting its d‐band center. This remote electronic activation lowers the activation barrier for H2 dissociation and fine-tunes the adsorption energies of reaction intermediates, thereby enhancing both the catalytic activity and selectivity (e.g. favoring the hydrogenation of the carbonyl group over full hydrogenation) compared with catalysts where the dopant is surface-exposed.
generation.material_initial_state: Cu nanoparticles dispersed on a silica support, doped with trace amounts (≈0.5 atom%) of Pt; initially synthesized under conditions that allow either preferential subsurface (metal–support interfacial) or surface exposure of Pt atoms.
generation.intervention: Prepare a controlled comparison by varying the post-synthesis treatment to force Pt atoms into either the subsurface (via mild H2 treatment at room temperature which promotes diffusion into the interface) or to remain surface-exposed (by avoiding such treatment). Carry out the hydrogenation of an unsaturated aldehyde such as cinnamaldehyde under identical reaction conditions.
generation.conditions: Gas-phase or liquid-phase hydrogenation reaction of unsaturated aldehydes under ambient pressure and moderate temperature, where H2 activation is rate-limiting and substrate adsorption is sensitive to the host metal’s electronic structure.
generation.structural_mediator: Subsurface Pt atoms alter the local electronic structure of nearby surface Cu atoms (by inducing a d-band center downshift of ~0.2–0.3 eV), which in turn governs the energy barriers for H2 activation and modulates the binding strength of adsorbed intermediates.
generation.mechanism: Remote electronic effects from interfacially embedded Pt atoms modify the density of states at the Fermi level of adjacent Cu surface atoms, leading to easier H2 dissociation and a balanced adsorption energy for reaction intermediates. This creates an environment that favors selective production of the unsaturated alcohol (via preferential hydrogenation of the C=O bond) rather than full hydrogenation that would occur if Pt were only surface-exposed.
generation.predicted_outcome: Catalysts with subsurface Pt will demonstrate lower activation energies for H2 dissociation (observable by lower onset potentials or faster reaction kinetics) and higher selectivity (e.g., higher ratio of unsaturated alcohol to over-hydrogenated products) compared with both pure Cu catalysts and those with surface-exposed Pt.
generation.baseline: Pure Cu catalysts and Pt-doped catalysts with predominantly surface-exposed Pt, which typically show modest activity/selectivity and may favor over-hydrogenation due to unmodulated adsorption characteristics.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic effect is expected to hold for dilute alloy catalysts (dopant <1 atom%) where the host metal (Cu) is supported on an inert oxide (such as silica) and for reactions wherein H2 activation is critical. It may not be applicable if higher dopant concentrations are used or if strong metal–support interactions override the remote activation effect.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis integrates findings from studies on Pt-doped Cu alloys (e.g., PMC11075014 results showing subsurface Pt affecting Cu electronic states) with principles of d-band engineering in alloy catalysts (as seen in studies like those on strain/d-band center tuning in Pd@PdAg nanocrystals from PMC9419203). The exact magnitude of the d-band shift and its translation to activity/selectivity improvements may depend on additional factors such as particle size, support morphology, and reaction conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of Cu–Pt catalysts with identical overall Pt content. In one set, employ a post-synthesis H2 treatment to drive Pt into the subsurface (ensuring formation of metal–support interfacial Pt) while in the other set, use conditions that retain Pt at the surface. Characterize the Pt location via in situ XAS or equivalent techniques. Then, perform catalytic hydrogenation of cinnamaldehyde under identical conditions. Measure reaction kinetics (e.g., activation energy, current density if electrochemical) and product distribution.
measurements: Determination of Pt atomic location (subsurface vs. surface) by in situ spectroscopic methods (XAS, XPS)
Kinetic parameters for H2 dissociation (e.g., onset potential, activation energy)
Product selectivity (ratio of unsaturated alcohol to over-hydrogenated products)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If catalysts with subsurface Pt do not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in the H2 activation barrier and do not show enhanced selectivity toward the unsaturated alcohol compared to both pure Cu and catalysts with surface-exposed Pt, then the remote electronic activation mechanism is not supported.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWith heterogeneous catalysts, chemical promotion takes place at their surfaces. Even in the case of single-atom alloys, where small quantities of a reactive metal are dispersed within the main host, it is assumed that both elements are exposed and available to bond with the reactants. Here, we show, on the basis of in situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy data, that in alloy catalysts made from Pt highly diluted in Cu the Pt atoms are located at the inner interface between the metal nanoparticles and the silica support instead. Kinetic experiments indicated that these catalysts still display better selectivity for the hydrogenation of unsaturated aldehydes to unsaturated alcohols than the pure metals. Density functional theory calculations corroborated the stability of Pt at the metal–support interface and explained the catalytic performance as being due to a remote lowering of the activation barrier for the dissociation of H2 at Cu sites by the internal Pt atoms.Keywords: single-atom alloy (SAA) catalysts; in situ studies; X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS, XANES, EXAFS); density functional theory (DFT); infrared absorption spectroscopy (IR); segregation; diffusion; hydrogen

The Pt atom is able to promote the activation of molecular hydrogen remotely because it affects the electronic structure of the Cu atoms at the surface of the cluster, even though it is several crystal lattice units away (two in the clusters used in our DFT calculations). This effect can be easily observed by the changes in the density of states (DOS) reported in Figure 4B (and in differential mode in Figure 4C). A couple of observations are worth highlighting from those results. First, the Pt substitution in the Cu25/SiO2(111) cluster at an inner NP/silica interface site induces a redistribution of the DOS in all of the Cu atoms (red traces), including in the surface Cu atom on which H2 adsorbs (vertex Cu; purple traces): there is a slight shift in the DOS between −1 and −2 eV toward the Fermi level, and additional electronic density develops around −3 eV at the vertex Cu. These changes contradict the general assumption that the d orbitals of the dopant metal in SAAs do not mix with those of the host metal and that therefore the dopant behaves as an isolated atom.
